newsitem.title: USA: UAW, Ford reach tentative contract agreement.
newsitem.headline: UAW, Ford reach tentative contract agreement.

text.p: After haggling over job security and parts subcontracting for nearly four days, Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers struck a tentative agreement Monday for a new national labour contract.
Union officials said the three-year pact guarantees jobs for about 95 percent of Ford's 105,000 hourly UAW workers, but other details were not immediately available.
UAW President Stephen Yokich would not discuss details of the pact, but said he expected ratification votes by Ford's workers to be completed by Sept. 29.
The union's executive board will review the pact on Tuesday, and the union's Ford council, made up of plant-level leaders, will consider the pact on Wednesday.

Analysts said the job guarantees showed that Ford was confident in its future growth. "Certainly for Ford they have to believe they are going to do well in terms of market share," said David Garrity, an analyst with Smith Barney & Co.
The pact came after marathon bargaining sessions over the weekend and on Monday. Ford's previous three-year contract with the UAW expired at midnight on Saturday.
"You can't imagine the hours that people have put in," Yokich said. "We were very tired last night. We went home and got some sleep because our jobs programme was in place."
Yokich also praised Ford Chairman Alex Trotman's direct involvement in the talks. "He's been involved. It used to be you had to go up to see the chairman, now he comes down to see you," Yokich said.
Trotman said pact benefits both the company and employees. "It's not a one-way street," he said.

The UAW has not decided yet whether to target General Motors Corp. or Chrysler Corp. for the next round of bargaining. He said the decision would be based partly on the outcome of Canadian talks with Chrysler.

The Canadian Auto Workers late Monday halted talks with Chrysler's Canadian unit because of a lack of progress on the key issue of shifting work to outside suppliers and warned that a strike looked more and more likely.
Canadian Auto Workers President Buzz Hargrove said it would now be difficult to conclude an agreement on all issues by the CAW's Tuesday strike deadline.
Yokich declined to say how the pact would affect GM or Chrysler, but he added that his goal all along was to reach agreements that all three automakers can live with.
"We're going after an agreement that all the companies can work with," he added.
Both Chrysler and GM said they had not seen specific details of the pact, and declined to comment on it. Talks had resumed at both automakers on Monday.

Analysts said the Ford deal could have a potentially greater impact on GM if the UAW enforces it as a pattern agreement. Industry observers estimate that GM needs to shed as much as 20 percent of its UAW hourly workers in order for its costs to become competitive with other automakers.
